case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may, consistent with the First Amendment, discipline licensed mental-health professionals for engaging in certain counseling conversations with minors—i.e., whether a generally applicable regulation of professional practice that restricts what a counselor can say is subject to heightened First Amendment scrutiny or treated as permissible regulation of professional conduct.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause) as applied to Colorado’s restriction on “conversion therapy”/sexual-orientation and gender-identity change efforts (SOCE) for minors by licensed mental-health professionals (enforced through Colorado’s professional-licensing regulatory scheme administered by the Department of Regulatory Agencies).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that Colorado’s ban functions as a content- and viewpoint-based speech restriction because it targets the substance and direction of counseling dialogue (permitting affirming conversations but penalizing change-oriented conversations). She contends that counseling is speech, not merely conduct, and that the State cannot evade strict (or at least heightened) scrutiny by relabeling speech as “professional conduct.” Petitioner further argues that the law censors therapeutic discussions sought by clients (and/or parents) and thereby chills protected expression within the counselor-client relationship, and that the State must satisfy the most demanding First Amendment standards to justify such a selective prohibition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the law is a permissible regulation of the practice of a licensed profession—i.e., regulation of professional conduct designed to protect minors from harmful or ineffective interventions—where any burden on speech is incidental to regulating treatment. They contend the State has broad authority to set standards of care and prohibit disfavored therapeutic practices for minors, and that the First Amendment does not create a right for professionals to provide a prohibited form of treatment simply because it is administered through words. On this view, the law should be reviewed under deferential standards applicable to professional regulation (or at most intermediate scrutiny) and upheld given the State’s interest in protecting minors’ health and welfare.
key_precedents: National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra (NIFLA) (2018)
Rumsfeld v. Forum for Academic & Institutional Rights, Inc. (FAIR) (2006)
Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey (1992) (informed-consent/disclosure context referenced in professional-speech debates)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is that Colorado’s line is drawn in expressly communicative terms—“affirming” versus “change-oriented”—and NIFLA warns against laundering a speech restriction through licensing labels. But NIFLA also reaffirmed the State’s traditional authority to regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, and in the narrow setting here—licensed counseling of minors within a fiduciary therapeutic relationship—the State is regulating a treatment modality as a standard of care rather than policing public debate or general advocacy. Reed’s content-discrimination framework, developed for laws regulating speech in the public sphere, is an awkward fit for individualized medical/mental-health treatment where the State has long prohibited harmful modalities even when administered through words; the better minimalist course is to uphold only as applied to licensed providers treating minors while expressly reserving adult counseling, general advocacy, and any statute that more clearly targets viewpoints. Casey’s informed-consent cases do not control, but they underscore that not every speech-involving regulation in the clinical context triggers strict scrutiny, and that history supports some latitude for States in protecting minors’ welfare through licensing standards.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow framing—that this is merely a standard-of-care rule regulating professional conduct with only incidental speech effects—does not withstand textual scrutiny because the statute’s operative trigger is the communicative content and direction of the counselor’s words, which is precisely the relabeling NIFLA cautioned against. Justice Kagan’s concern that applying Reed in the therapeutic setting would destabilize ordinary licensing regimes is a policy objection that cannot supply a First Amendment carveout absent a historically grounded exception in the Constitution’s original public meaning. Casey’s informed-consent line, which Roberts and Kagan invoke, involves compelled factual disclosures ancillary to a medical procedure, not a categorical ban on disfavored counseling viewpoints in a private conversation, so it does not justify this viewpoint-discriminatory regime. As Justice Gorsuch and Justice Alito emphasize, the State may pursue child-protection through neutral malpractice standards and evidentiary showings of harm, but it may not selectively suppress one side of a therapeutic dialogue based on its viewpoint.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that NIFLA preserves State authority to regulate professional conduct that only incidentally involves speech, especially in a fiduciary setting with minors, and that Reed’s public-forum frame is an awkward fit. But this statute does not merely incidentally burden speech while regulating a separately describable act; it defines the proscribed “treatment” by the content and direction of what the counselor says—allowing “affirming” dialogue while forbidding “change-oriented” dialogue—which is precisely the kind of relabeling NIFLA warned against and looks like viewpoint discrimination in operation. Casey’s informed-consent line (invoked by Roberts/Kagan) concerns compelled factual disclosures ancillary to a procedure, not a categorical suppression of one side of a contested therapeutic conversation, so it does not supply a historically grounded carveout here. Federalism and administrability concerns cannot justify empowering licensing boards to punish disfavored viewpoints rather than insisting on neutral malpractice standards tied to demonstrated harm.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett press the strongest objection: the statute is drafted in directional, message-based terms that looks like viewpoint discrimination under Reed and the relabeling concern in NIFLA. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, NIFLA rejected a broad “professional speech” carveout while still preserving State authority to regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, and this fits a historically familiar lane—licensing discipline for a defined treatment modality applied to minors in a fiduciary therapeutic relationship. Reed’s framework, built for public-facing regulation of expression, maps poorly onto confidential, client-specific treatment where the State is defining standards of care to prevent harm to children, not policing public debate; treating every talk-therapy modality rule as strict-scrutiny censorship would destabilize routine health-and-safety regulation and undercut access to safe care for vulnerable minors. I would maintain our narrow posture—upholding as applied to licensed counseling of minors and reserving broader applications—rather than constitutionalizing a right to provide an intervention the State reasonably deems harmful simply because it is administered through words.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas are right to press that the statute’s definitions track communicative content and “direction,” which creates a serious Reed/NIFLA risk if we treat the counseling room like a public forum and presume strict scrutiny whenever a rule can be phrased in message-based terms. But as the Chief Justice argues, NIFLA’s central warning was against a categorical “professional speech” carveout, not against States’ historically grounded authority to define and prohibit a treatment modality for minors through licensing standards where the regulation targets professional practice and any speech burden is derivative of that practice. Reed’s anti-content-discrimination framework fits awkwardly in a fiduciary, client-specific therapeutic relationship where the State is not structuring public debate but setting a standard of care to prevent harm to children, and adopting petitioners’ view risks constitutionalizing a right to deliver any disfavored modality so long as it is administered through words. I would therefore uphold narrowly as applied to licensed providers treating minors, while reserving whether different applications (adults, general advocacy, or a statute untethered from a defined treatment modality) would present a viewpoint-discrimination problem.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right to emphasize NIFLA’s recognition that States may regulate professional conduct that only incidentally involves speech, and that Reed’s public-forum machinery can fit awkwardly in a fiduciary therapeutic setting. But this statute is not a neutral standard-of-care rule with incidental speech effects; it defines the forbidden “treatment” by the communicative content and directional message of the counseling—allowing “affirming” talk while banning “change-oriented” talk—so the State’s trigger for discipline is speech and viewpoint, precisely the relabeling NIFLA warned against. Casey’s informed-consent cases (factual disclosures tied to a procedure) do not supply an analogous historical or doctrinal exception for outright suppression of disfavored counseling dialogue. However weighty Colorado’s child-protection interests, under our First Amendment precedents they must be pursued through viewpoint-neutral malpractice and evidentiary standards, not by licensing boards acting as censors of particular ideas in private conversations.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the statute’s strongest flaw: its disciplinary trigger is defined in communicative, directional terms, which looks like content—and arguably viewpoint—discrimination under Reed and invites NIFLA’s warning against relabeling speech bans as “professional regulation.” But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that Reed’s public-forum template is a poor fit for a confidential, fiduciary treatment relationship involving minors where States have traditionally set standards of care through licensing, even for talk-based modalities. NIFLA matters here because it rejects a free-floating “professional speech” discount, yet it simultaneously preserves regulation of professional conduct that incidentally involves speech; on that historical and institutionalist understanding, this law is closer to regulating a treatment modality for minors than policing public debate. Justice Alito’s slippery-slope concern is serious, but the administrable limiting principle is the narrow, licensure-based application to minors’ treatment and the absence of any restriction on general advocacy or adult counseling, which meaningfully cabins the censorship risk.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s strongest contention—that this is a standard-of-care regulation of professional conduct that only incidentally involves speech—does not fit the statutory design, because Colorado defines the forbidden “treatment” by the communicative content and direction of the counselor’s message (change-oriented versus affirming), making speech the trigger for liability. NIFLA is directly relevant here: it rejected a “professional speech” carveout and warned that States may not repackage speech restrictions as licensing rules, while still allowing regulation of conduct with incidental speech effects—this statute falls in the former category. Casey and FAIR, which Roberts and Kagan invoke, concern compelled factual disclosures or conduct rules where speech is ancillary; they do not supply an historically grounded exception for viewpoint-based suppression of counseling dialogue. Even accepting the federalism and administrability concerns Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, the First Amendment’s baseline against content and viewpoint discrimination remains, and the State must pursue child-protection through neutral malpractice standards rather than censoring disfavored therapeutic viewpoints.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Thomas press the statute’s hardest point: the trigger for discipline is framed in communicative, directional terms (change-oriented vs affirming), raising real Reed/NIFLA risks of viewpoint discrimination laundered through licensing. But NIFLA’s key limitation is that it rejected a free-floating “professional speech” category, while still preserving historically grounded authority to regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech; as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, this fits a standards-of-care rule for licensed treatment of minors in a fiduciary therapeutic relationship, not a public-debate speech code. Reed’s public-forum content-discrimination template is a poor fit for individualized healthcare regulation, and importing strict scrutiny mechanically would constitutionalize talk-based treatment modalities and destabilize routine state licensing oversight. I would therefore uphold narrowly as applied to licensed counseling of minors, while expressly reserving (as Roberts and Kagan suggest) that a broader law or one deployed to punish general advocacy or adults could present a different, potentially viewpoint-discriminatory case.

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction is best understood as a regulation of the practice of a licensed profession—setting a standard of care for treatment of minors—rather than a freestanding censorship of public debate, and any burden on speech arises because the treatment is administered through words. Under NIFLA v. Becerra, we declined to recognize a special “professional speech” category, but reaffirmed that States may regulate “professional conduct” that “incidentally involves speech,” and we have long tolerated malpractice- and informed-consent-style regulation within the “traditional purview of state regulation of professional conduct.” 585 U.S. 755, 768–70 (2018) (quoting Casey, 505 U.S. at 884). Consistent with institutional restraint and federalism, I would uphold this narrow, generally applicable licensing rule for minors’ care without announcing broad First Amendment doctrine beyond what NIFLA already supplies. On this record, Colorado’s interest in protecting minors’ health and welfare suffices under the applicable, deferential review of professional conduct regulations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction disciplines licensed counselors based on the content and viewpoint of what they say in the counseling room—permitting “affirming” speech while prohibiting change-oriented counseling—so it triggers heightened (indeed, strict) scrutiny under the First Amendment’s text as originally understood and this Court’s content-based doctrine. In NIFLA v. Becerra, 585 U.S. 755 (2018), we rejected any free-floating “professional speech” category that would let States evade ordinary First Amendment rules simply by regulating a licensed profession, and Reed v. Town of Gilbert, 576 U.S. 155 (2015), confirms that content-based speech regulations are presumptively unconstitutional. Unlike Rumsfeld v. FAIR, 547 U.S. 47 (2006), this law does not primarily regulate conduct with only incidental speech effects; it directly regulates speech itself by banning particular counseling conversations. Because Colorado has chosen censorship rather than regulating professional conduct through generally applicable standards of care, the discipline scheme cannot stand under the Free Speech Clause.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Colorado’s SOCE ban is triggered by the content and viewpoint of what the licensed counselor says in the counseling room—permitting “affirming” dialogue but punishing “change-oriented” dialogue—so it is a content-based regulation of speech under the First Amendment. NIFLA rejected any freestanding, diminished-protection category of “professional speech” and cautioned that States may not evade heightened scrutiny merely by labeling speech as professional conduct; this statute looks like precisely that sort of relabeling. Unlike compelled factual disclosures in the informed-consent setting referenced in Casey, Colorado is prohibiting a class of counseling conversations because of their message, and under Reed such content discrimination demands at least heightened scrutiny. Given the practical consequences of allowing States to suppress disfavored therapeutic viewpoints through licensing sanctions, the law cannot be sustained without the demanding justification the First Amendment requires.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as a regulation of licensed professional practice aimed at protecting minors from a treatment the State has deemed harmful, and any impact on speech is incidental to regulating conduct within the therapeutic relationship. NIFLA rejected a freestanding “professional speech” carveout, but it reaffirmed that States may regulate “professional conduct” that “incidentally involves speech,” citing Casey’s approval of certain medical disclosures as part of practice. Unlike the compelled or ideological speech problems in NIFLA and Reed, this law sets a standard of care for licensed providers treating minors and fits within the State’s traditional authority to discipline professional misconduct through its licensing scheme. Given the practical stakes for vulnerable minors and the State’s protective interest, heightened scrutiny is not required on this record and the law should be upheld.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction is best understood as a generally applicable standard-of-care rule governing the practice of a licensed profession with respect to minors, even though the treatment is administered through words. Under NIFLA, the Court rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category but reaffirmed that States may regulate “professional conduct” that “incidentally involves speech,” including in contexts like informed-consent and professional standards. Unlike the compelled-speech problem in NIFLA, this law targets a defined therapeutic intervention and is administered through ordinary licensing discipline, a domain where States have long had room to set and enforce minimum standards for health and safety. Given the State’s strong interest in protecting minors and the workability of treating this as professional-conduct regulation rather than content-based censorship, heightened First Amendment scrutiny is not required here and the law may be upheld.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Colorado’s law disciplines licensed counselors based on the content and viewpoint of what they say in the counseling room—permitting “affirming” dialogue while prohibiting “change-oriented” dialogue—triggering heightened First Amendment scrutiny under Reed v. Town of Gilbert. NIFLA rejected any freestanding “professional speech” exception and cautioned that a State may not evade ordinary First Amendment review by recharacterizing speech as professional conduct, even while recognizing limited space for regulating professional conduct with only incidental effects on speech. Here, the State has not merely set a generally applicable standard of care or required disclosures (cf. Casey); it has singled out a particular subject and direction of speech for punishment, which cannot be sustained absent the most demanding justification. Separation-of-powers and rule-of-law concerns counsel against allowing licensing boards to enforce viewpoint-based orthodoxy through discipline, especially where the regulation operates as censorship rather than malpractice liability for demonstrable harm.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as a regulation of the practice of a licensed profession directed at protecting minors’ health and welfare, and any burden on speech arises from regulating a professional treatment modality administered within the counselor–client relationship. Under NIFLA v. Becerra, the Court declined to recognize a freestanding “professional speech” category but reaffirmed that States may regulate “professional conduct” that incidentally involves speech, including within the course of medical or therapeutic treatment (citing Casey’s informed-consent framework). Consistent with that history-and-tradition understanding of professional licensing and standards of care, and mindful of workability and institutional legitimacy, I would not constitutionalize a right to provide a prohibited treatment simply because it is delivered through words. The First Amendment does not require strict scrutiny for this kind of generally applicable standard-of-care regulation of licensed practice involving minors.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction targets what may be said in counseling sessions based on the topic (sexual orientation/gender identity change efforts) and the direction of the message (change-oriented versus affirming), making it a content-based—and plausibly viewpoint-based—speech regulation subject to heightened scrutiny under the First Amendment. NIFLA rejected any freestanding “professional speech” carveout and cautioned that States may not evade ordinary First Amendment rules by labeling speech as professional regulation, permitting only narrow exceptions (e.g., regulation of professional conduct that only incidentally burdens speech and certain disclosure requirements). Unlike Casey’s informed-consent disclosures or FAIR’s regulation of conduct with incidental speech effects, this law directly prohibits particular counseling conversations because of their communicative content, and thus must satisfy at least strict scrutiny, which the State has not shown on this record. Because the statute disciplines licensed professionals for speech in the counselor-client relationship based on its content and viewpoint, the First Amendment requires more than deferential review applicable to general standards-of-care regulation.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as a generally applicable standard-of-care rule governing the professional treatment of minors, and any impact on speech is incidental to regulating the practice of a licensed profession aimed at preventing harm to children. Under NIFLA, the Court has not created a free-standing “professional speech” category, but it also recognizes that States may impose reasonable regulations tied to professional conduct and treatment, especially within a client-specific therapeutic relationship rather than public-facing compelled speech. Consistent with the regulatory tradition reflected in Casey’s informed-consent framework and this Court’s conduct/speech line in FAIR, Colorado may prohibit a disfavored therapeutic intervention for minors without triggering strict scrutiny merely because the intervention is delivered through words. Given the State’s substantial interest in protecting minors’ health and welfare through licensing enforcement, the law should be upheld under at most intermediate scrutiny (or a deferential reasonableness approach for treatment regulations).

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may, consistent with the First Amendment, discipline licensed mental-health professionals for the content of what they say in counseling sessions with minors—specifically when the counseling is intended to reduce or change same-sex attractions or gender-related behaviors.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause) as applied to Colorado’s prohibition on licensed mental-health providers engaging in ‘conversion therapy’ (i.e., counseling efforts aimed at changing sexual orientation or gender identity) with minors.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner argues that Colorado’s law is a content- and viewpoint-based restriction on speech because it targets particular counseling messages (those favoring change or reduction of same-sex attraction or gender dysphoria) while allowing the opposite messages, and therefore must survive strict scrutiny. She contends the State cannot re-label speech as ‘professional conduct’ to evade heightened First Amendment review, especially after the Court’s rejection of a distinct, lesser-protected category of ‘professional speech.’ Petitioner (and supporting amici) emphasize that talk therapy is overwhelmingly speech, that the law discriminates among viewpoints in a sensitive moral and political debate, and that existing licensing and malpractice frameworks can address genuinely harmful practices without banning disfavored ideas.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue the law is a permissible regulation of professional conduct within the State’s licensing authority, aimed at protecting minors from harmful practices, with only incidental effects on speech. They contend the State may set standards of care and bar treatments it deems unsafe or ineffective, including certain therapeutic interventions delivered through words. Respondents (and supporting amici) frame the restriction as part of regulating the practice of mental health counseling rather than suppressing ideas, and maintain that the law should be reviewed under a more deferential standard than strict scrutiny because it governs professional practice with vulnerable clients.
key_precedents: National Institute of Family & Life Advocates v. Becerra (NIFLA) (2018)
R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul (1992)
Planned Parenthood of Southeastern Pennsylvania v. Casey (1992)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the State may set standards of care for minors and that, under NIFLA, regulation of professional conduct can incidentally affect speech; that child-protection interest carries real weight. But as Justice Kagan candidly recognizes, this statute’s operative trigger is the communicative aim—counseling “to reduce or change” versus counseling that affirms—so in a talk-therapy setting speech is not incidental to the treatment but the treatment itself, bringing Reed and R.A.V. squarely to the fore. Casey’s informed-consent line, as Justice Thomas notes, concerns compelled disclosures tethered to a medical procedure and does not license a categorical, message-based ban in a speech-only therapeutic modality. A narrow disposition invalidating this viewpoint-tilted prohibition—while leaving room for generally applicable malpractice, coercion/fraud rules, and evidence-based discipline—best preserves First Amendment doctrine without constitutionalizing every clinical standard and better serves institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point—that this is merely a standard-of-care regulation of professional conduct for minors with only incidental effects on speech under NIFLA—fails because the statute defines the prohibited “practice” by communicative content and purpose (counseling intended to “reduce or change”), while permitting the opposite message, which triggers Reed/R.A.V. content- and viewpoint-discrimination concerns. Justice Kagan’s worry that applying heightened scrutiny here would destabilize ordinary psychotherapy standards is overstated: generally applicable malpractice rules and evidence-based, conduct-focused regulations remain available, but a categorical ban drawn by message cannot be justified by administrative convenience or labeling it “treatment.” Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis that, in talk therapy, speech is the treatment underscores that NIFLA’s conduct/incidental-speech lane cannot be stretched to create a de facto “professional speech” carveout NIFLA rejected. Casey’s informed-consent decisions do not support suppressing one side of a contested moral debate in a speech-only setting untethered to a procedure.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan offer the best response: characterize this as a standard-of-care rule for minors, regulating professional conduct with only incidental speech effects under NIFLA and in the spirit of Casey. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress, in talk therapy speech is the treatment, and Colorado defines the forbidden “practice” by communicative purpose and content—counseling aimed to “reduce or change” specified feelings—while permitting the opposite counseling, which squarely triggers Reed and R.A.V.’s content/viewpoint-discrimination concerns. NIFLA rejected a discounted “professional speech” category, and Casey’s compelled, procedure-tethered disclosure rationale does not support a categorical ban on one side of a contested moral question in a speech-only setting. The State can protect minors through generally applicable malpractice, coercion/fraud prohibitions, and case-specific discipline, which underscores the lack of narrow tailoring for this message-based restriction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s point that “speech is the treatment” in talk therapy, and thus Reed/R.A.V. concerns are not easily avoided, is the strongest argument on the other side and it forces care about chilling effects and administrability. But it still does not defeat the State’s traditional licensing authority, preserved in NIFLA, to set standards of care for minors in a fiduciary therapeutic relationship where the State is targeting a treatment objective (directed change efforts) rather than suppressing an idea in the public sphere; many clinical prohibitions are necessarily articulated in communicative terms without becoming ordinary marketplace-of-ideas censorship. Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch overread Reed/R.A.V. by treating purpose-based clinical line-drawing as per se viewpoint discrimination, even though the law can be narrowed to reach only intentional, intervention-like efforts to change identity/orientation while leaving exploration, support, and discussion untouched. I would therefore uphold on the understanding (as Justice Jackson stresses) that a limiting construction and clear enforcement safeguards are essential to prevent the statute from sweeping in neutral counseling or open-ended patient-led dialogue.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Thomas’s strongest point is that the statute’s trigger—counseling “to reduce or change” rather than to affirm—looks like Reed/R.A.V. content (and maybe viewpoint) discrimination, and NIFLA warned us not to invent a discounted “professional speech” category. But I do not think those cases translate cleanly to a licensed fiduciary treatment relationship with minors where the State is defining a prohibited therapeutic objective as a standard-of-care rule; under NIFLA’s preserved lane for regulating “professional conduct that incidentally involves speech,” many treatment modalities are necessarily communicative without becoming ordinary public-debate speech. The petitioners’ proposed “narrow disposition” would, as a practical matter, constitutionalize heightened scrutiny whenever a medical or psychological standard is articulated in communicative terms, destabilizing routine licensing regulation and malpractice baselines in psychotherapy. The better approach is a narrowing construction and application focused on directed change efforts as a clinical intervention, while making clear that exploratory, supportive, identity-neutral counseling and public advocacy remain protected.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Kagan offer the strongest counter: that Colorado is simply setting a standard of care for minors and thus regulating professional conduct with only incidental effects on speech under NIFLA. But NIFLA rejected a free-floating “professional speech” carveout, and its conduct/incidental-speech lane does not fit a law that defines the forbidden “practice” by communicative aim—counseling intended “to reduce or change”—while permitting the opposite counseling; that is classic Reed/R.A.V. content and viewpoint discrimination in a context where speech is the treatment. Casey’s informed-consent precedents (as Chief Justice Roberts notes) involved compelled, procedure-tethered disclosures, not a categorical ban on one side of a contested moral question delivered through talk therapy. Even crediting the State’s child-protection interest, narrow tailoring is lacking because Colorado can address coercion, fraud, and demonstrable harm through generally applicable malpractice and targeted discipline without prohibiting disfavored viewpoints ex ante.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Sotomayor offer the strongest counter: that Colorado is setting a standard of care for minors within a licensed fiduciary relationship, and NIFLA preserves regulation of professional conduct that incidentally involves speech. But as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, this statute does not merely describe a care standard; it defines the forbidden “practice” by the communicative objective—counseling aimed at “reducing or changing” while allowing counseling that affirms—placing it squarely in Reed/R.A.V. content- and viewpoint-discrimination territory in a domain where speech is the treatment, not incidental. Casey’s informed-consent line is not a workable analogy because it involved procedure-tethered disclosures, not a categorical ban on one side of a contested question, and the availability of less speech-restrictive tools (malpractice, fraud/coercion prohibitions, case-specific discipline) undercuts narrow tailoring even crediting the State’s child-protection interest. Institutionally, a narrow holding invalidating this viewpoint-tilted prohibition while preserving room for evidence-based, conduct-focused regulation best fits our precedents and avoids creating a de facto “professional speech” exception NIFLA rejected.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point is that many psychotherapy standards necessarily describe communicative techniques and so fit within NIFLA’s allowance for regulating “professional conduct that incidentally involves speech,” especially for minors. But this statute does not merely regulate a technique or impose a generally applicable competence rule; it defines the forbidden “practice” by the content and aim of the words—counseling “to reduce or change” specified attractions/behaviors—while allowing counseling with the opposite objective, which Chief Justice Roberts correctly notes pulls us into Reed and R.A.V. territory where strict scrutiny is the baseline. Casey’s informed-consent framework does not extend to a talk-only setting in which speech is the treatment and the State bars one side of a contested moral question rather than tethering disclosures to a procedure. Even crediting the State’s compelling interest in protecting minors, Colorado’s availability of malpractice, fraud/coercion prohibitions, and individualized discipline underscores the lack of narrow tailoring for a categorical, message-based ban.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Alito’s strongest point is that, in talk therapy, speech is the treatment, and this statute’s trigger—counseling aimed “to reduce or change” versus not—has Reed/R.A.V. surface features of content (and perhaps viewpoint) discrimination that NIFLA warns us not to evade via a “professional speech” discount. But I still think that framing misdescribes what Colorado is doing: it is regulating a defined clinical intervention within a licensed, fiduciary relationship with minors, a setting where the State’s traditional police power to set baseline standards of care (recognized in NIFLA’s conduct/incidental-speech lane) carries special weight because the practical consequence of waiting for individualized malpractice is preventable harm to children. Reed and R.A.V. are not a perfect doctrinal fit because the State is not selecting among ideas in public discourse; it is drawing a boundary around a treatment objective it deems harmful/ineffective for minors, while leaving room for exploratory, supportive, and identity-neutral counseling. Still, I agree with Roberts that narrowing construction and procedural safeguards are essential to reduce chilling effects and ensure enforcement targets only directed change efforts, not ordinary therapeutic discussion.

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado’s statute disciplines licensed counselors based on the content—and effectively the viewpoint—of what is said in a therapy session, permitting counseling that affirms same-sex attraction or gender transition while forbidding counseling aimed at reducing or changing those feelings, which triggers heightened First Amendment concern under Reed v. Town of Gilbert and R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul. Under NIFLA, we rejected a freestanding “professional speech” category that would dilute First Amendment protection simply because speech occurs in a professional setting; while States may regulate professional conduct and impose malpractice standards, a broad ban that turns on the message conveyed is not easily recast as mere conduct regulation. A narrow ruling is available: Colorado may enforce evidence-based standards of care and prohibit coercive or harmful practices through generally applicable malpractice and licensing rules, but this content-based prohibition on in-session counseling speech to minors cannot stand on the current justification. Protecting minors is a compelling interest, but the State has not shown this speech-targeted ban is narrowly tailored when less speech-restrictive professional regulations are available.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Colorado’s ban disciplines licensed counselors based on the content and viewpoint of what is said in counseling sessions—permitting affirming discussions while prohibiting counseling aimed at reducing same-sex attraction or gender-related behaviors—triggering strict scrutiny under the First Amendment. Under Reed v. Town of Gilbert and R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul, the State may not impose content- or viewpoint-based restrictions on speech absent the most compelling justification, and it cannot evade that rule by relabeling disfavored speech as “professional conduct.” NIFLA rejected a freestanding lesser-protected category of “professional speech” and cautioned that speech does not lose protection merely because it occurs in a professional-client relationship; whatever room Casey leaves for informed-consent regulations, this law is not a disclosure requirement but a direct ban on particular viewpoints expressed through talk therapy. On an original public meaning understanding of the Free Speech Clause and consistent with our precedents, Colorado’s licensing power does not authorize suppressing disfavored ideas in a contested moral and political domain.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Colorado’s prohibition turns on what the counselor says and the viewpoint the counselor conveys—permitting counseling that affirms same-sex attraction or a gender transition while forbidding counseling aimed at reducing or changing those feelings—making it a content- and viewpoint-based restriction presumptively subject to strict scrutiny under Reed v. Town of Gilbert and R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul. The State cannot evade that scrutiny by relabeling a speech ban as regulation of “professional conduct,” because NIFLA rejected a distinct, lesser-protected category of “professional speech” and made clear that content-based burdens on speech by licensed professionals generally receive ordinary First Amendment review. While States have broad authority to regulate the practice of medicine, disciplining a therapist for the content of talk therapy is not merely “incidental” to regulating conduct; it is the regulation, and Colorado has less restrictive tools (licensing discipline for fraud, coercion, or malpractice) to address genuine harms. Even accepting the State’s interest in protecting minors, the law’s viewpoint discrimination and breadth make it difficult to justify under the First Amendment as applied here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction is best understood as a regulation of licensed professional conduct in the provision of mental-health treatment to minors, a setting where the State has heightened authority to set and enforce standards of care to protect a vulnerable population. Under NIFLA v. Becerra, the Court rejected a free-floating “professional speech” carveout but reaffirmed that States may regulate professional conduct that incidentally involves speech, including prohibiting substandard treatment delivered through words. The law targets a therapeutic practice the State deems harmful or ineffective for minors rather than suppressing ideas in public discourse, akin to the State’s ability to require or forbid certain medical disclosures or interventions within the clinical relationship recognized in Planned Parenthood v. Casey. Given the real-world risks to minors and the State’s licensing power, heightened First Amendment scrutiny is not warranted simply because the treatment modality is talk therapy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction is best understood as a regulation of the professional practice of licensed mental-health counseling with minors—i.e., a standard-of-care rule—rather than a general attempt to suppress ideas in public discourse. NIFLA rejected a free-floating “professional speech” category, but it reaffirmed that States may regulate “professional conduct that incidentally involves speech,” particularly in the medical context, consistent with Casey’s recognition that certain provider-patient communications may be required or constrained as part of practice. Given the State’s traditional licensing authority and its interest in protecting minors from treatments it deems harmful or ineffective, intermediate/deferential review is appropriate and the law is workable as a conduct rule even though it operates through words. Reed and R.A.V. underscore the danger of content/viewpoint discrimination, but in this setting the statute targets a therapeutic intervention (conversion therapy) within a defined professional relationship, not advocacy generally, making it closer to permissible regulation of professional conduct than to viewpoint-based censorship.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Colorado’s prohibition singles out speech in the counseling room based on its content and viewpoint—barring efforts “to reduce or change” same-sex attraction or gender-related behaviors while permitting counseling that affirms or encourages them—triggering strict scrutiny under Reed v. Town of Gilbert and R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul. NIFLA rejected a freestanding, lesser-protected category of “professional speech,” and a State may not evade the First Amendment by relabeling disfavored talk therapy as mere “professional conduct.” While the State retains authority to regulate malpractice and to require informed consent, a categorical ban on a particular viewpoint in a sensitive moral and political debate is not the narrow tailoring the Free Speech Clause demands. Because the law suppresses a disfavored message rather than regulating nonexpressive conduct, it cannot stand.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Colorado’s ban, as applied to talk therapy, turns on the content and viewpoint of what the counselor says—permitting counseling that affirms same-sex attraction or gender transition while forbidding counseling aimed at reducing same-sex attraction or gender-related behaviors—triggering strict scrutiny under Reed v. Town of Gilbert and R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul. NIFLA rejects a freestanding “professional speech” category and cautions that States may not evade First Amendment review by relabeling speech as professional conduct; this law is not a mere regulation of conduct with incidental speech effects. Although the State has a weighty interest in protecting minors, the categorical prohibition on specified counseling viewpoints is difficult to square with our speech precedents and may be pursued through less speech-restrictive licensing and malpractice tools. Consistent with institutional concerns and workability, the First Amendment does not permit disciplining licensed professionals based on disfavored counseling messages absent the most exacting justification.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Colorado’s law disciplines licensed counselors based on the communicative content and viewpoint of what is said in a counseling session—prohibiting efforts to reduce same-sex attraction or gender-related behaviors while permitting the opposite counsel—triggering the First Amendment’s rule that content- and viewpoint-based restrictions are presumptively unconstitutional. Under Reed v. Town of Gilbert and R.A.V. v. City of St. Paul, the State cannot discriminate among viewpoints in a contested moral and political debate, and NIFLA rejects a freestanding, lesser-protected category of “professional speech” that would dilute ordinary First Amendment scrutiny for talk-based counseling. Although the State may regulate professional conduct and standards of care, NIFLA’s conduct/incidental-speech principle (and Casey’s informed-consent context) does not fit a regime that targets the message itself rather than requiring disclosures or regulating nonexpressive treatment modalities. Because the statute is best characterized as a content- and viewpoint-based speech restriction, it must satisfy strict scrutiny, which is unlikely on this record given the availability of less speech-restrictive alternatives through licensing, malpractice, and case-specific discipline.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Colorado’s restriction operates as a regulation of licensed professional conduct—setting a standard of care for treatment of minors—even if the treatment is delivered through words, and thus any burden on speech is incidental to the State’s traditional authority to protect patients and discipline unsafe practices. NIFLA v. Becerra rejected a free-floating “professional speech” carveout but reaffirmed that States may regulate “professional conduct” that “incidentally involves speech,” citing Casey’s approval of informed-consent-type regulation within the practice of medicine. Given minors’ vulnerability and the State’s asserted interest in preventing harm, the statute fits within the State’s licensing and malpractice framework rather than a public-forum-style viewpoint censorship, and strict scrutiny is not compelled simply because the therapy is talk-based. In light of the practical consequences and procedural fairness concerns in regulating clinical treatment for children, I would uphold Colorado’s law as a permissible standard-of-care measure under the First Amendment.
